### 6.1 Smoked Brisket

**Cody's own brisket, dictated 2026-09-08 — the straight-smoke method, and the placeholder this entry carried for months is now closed.** The shape of it: **salt it heavy the night before and leave it in the fridge overnight**, then **coarse ground black pepper** the next day — *"it has never let me down"* — **pit at 225°F, let it settle a full hour, a handful of pecan, and wait for the blue smoke** before the meat goes anywhere near it. Then a probe in it: **165°F, let it stall, and wrap it in foil** — **or don't wrap it at all**, the way Meathead does, for a better bark. Both of those are his, and he's up front about where the method comes from: *"it's kind of really the Meathead method, actually. I don't know that I've done anything different, but I don't like his Big Bad Beef Rub."* **And he names its one real weakness himself: on a straight smoke he has no control over when it gets done.** That is the entire reason [§6.10 Sous Vide Brisket (Richie's Method)](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) exists, and the two entries should be read as a pair.

**❤️ Family favorite** — *Cody: "Awesome."*

> ⚠️🧂 **THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS PAGE — DON'T SALT IT TWICE. Read this before you buy a rub.** This is Cody's own warning and it is the sharpest thing in the method: **if the rub you're using already has salt in it, do NOT also dry brine with salt.** Two things go wrong at once. **It comes out too salty** — you have seasoned the same piece of meat twice, at full strength, both times. **And most of that second dose of salt never penetrates anyway**, so you've paid the saltiness price without getting the benefit; a rub thrown on shortly before the cook sits on the surface, where [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md)'s own numbers say salt travels less than an inch in a full day of *dedicated* brining time.
>
> **So pick one of these two, and commit to it:**
>
> | | **Path A — plain salt, then an unsalted seasoning** *(what Cody does)* | **Path B — a salted rub, applied the night before** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Night before** | **Plain kosher salt only**, heavy, into the fridge | **The salted rub itself**, on the meat, into the fridge |
> | **Next day** | **An UNSALTED seasoning** — for Cody, coarse black pepper and nothing else | Nothing more, or a little extra pepper |
> | **Why it works** | The salt has all night to get in; the seasoning is pure flavor on top | The rub's salt is *doing* the dry brine, so it gets the night it needs |
> | **The failure** | Reaching for a salted rub the next morning out of habit | Adding a salt dry brine underneath it as well |
>
> **The rule in one line, in his terms: if you dry brined with plain salt, whatever goes on afterward must be unsalted. If your rub carries the salt, put it on the night before so the salt has time to work.**
>
> **This cookbook is full of both kinds, so check before you reach.** [§4.105 Dalmatian Rub](4105-dalmatian-rub.md) and Cody's own salt-and-pepper Dalmatian in [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) are **salted** — night-before rubs. Every Meathead rub here is **salt-free by design** ([§T53](t53-the-science-of-a-good-rub--three-ss-no-salt-in-rubs-and-storage.md), [§T90](t90-the-five-ss-of-a-rub-sugar-wariness-and-no-salt-the-meathead-method.md)) and is meant to go *on top of* a separate dry brine — that's Path A. And [§6.7 Texas-Style Barbecued Brisket](67-texas-style-barbecued-brisket.md)'s seasoning, the one Cody has read and signed off on, carries **1 Tbsp of coarse salt in it** — so it's a Path B rub, and the 4-to-8-hour cure printed with it *is* the dry brine. Don't put a salt brine underneath it.

**Techniques used:** [§T37 Salt, Brining, and the Dry Brine](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md) *(the overnight salting **is** the dry brine — the Roberts Way, heavy, every time)* · [§T35 Smoke Science](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md) *(blue smoke, and **Cody's palmful-of-wood rule**)* · [§T69 Brisket Basics](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md) *(what a packer is, and how to buy one)* · [§T70 Slicing Brisket](t70-slicing-brisket--the-easy-way-vs-the-sorkin-way.md) · [§T44 Food Safety — Target Temperatures](t44-food-safety--the-real-logic-and-the-target-temperature-table.md) · [§T33 How Meat Actually Cooks](t33-how-meat-actually-cooks--conduction-carryover-and-why-resting-is-a-myth.md) *(the stall)* · [§T43 Faux Cambro](t43-faux-cambro--holding-meat-hot-for-hours.md) · [§T40 The Fat Cap — Trim or Not](t40-the-fat-cap--trim-or-not.md) · [§T109 Indirect Heat](t109-indirect-heat--putting-something-between-the-fire-and-the-food.md)

**🟢 Easy** · **Prep ~15 min** *(the salting the night before, then the pepper the next day)* · **Slow cook ~12–14 hr** *(225°F indirect, unattended — plus about an hour for the pit to settle **before** the meat goes on)* · **Start to finish ~1½ days** *(includes the overnight dry brine, and a rest after — see Step 6)*

**⏰ Countdown to dinner:** T−1½ days (the night before) salt it heavy, plain kosher, into the fridge overnight — nothing salted goes on after this · T−15 to 17 hr (the morning of) coarse black pepper over everything; fire the pit to 225°F indirect and let it settle a full hour · T−14 to 16 hr a palmful of pecan, wait for thin blue smoke, brisket on with the leave-in probe — 12–14 hr (cookbook figure from [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md), labelled in the entry); at about 165°F wrap tight in foil, or don't · at 203°F off and into the cooler, no ice · T−10 min slice across the grain as you serve · *(offsets count a 2 hr cooler rest — §7.112's at-least-2-hr hold, chosen here because Cody's own brisket rest is not stated; see Open Questions)*.

> **Why this is 🟢 Easy, and it's the same call as [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md).** [CLAUDE.md §3a](../../CLAUDE.md)'s test is the only one that counts: *can a step go from perfect to ruined?* **Walk it.** Salting a brisket and putting it in the fridge can't fail. Grinding pepper on it can't fail. Bringing a pit to 225°F and letting it settle an hour can't fail — that hour exists precisely so nothing has to be rushed. The twelve hours that follow are the smoker's work, and the stall, which is the longest and most maddening stretch, tests patience and nothing else. Wrapping or not wrapping is a **choice with a tradeoff**, not a step you can botch. **Nothing here has a one-minute window.** *(Contrast with the actual 🔴 cases in this book — a dark roux, where a minute of inattention means starting over.)* **Long is not hard**: twelve hours of hands-off smoke is exactly what the Slow cook field is for, and per [§1 Cody's Pho](1-codys-pho.md) — *it's a long distance run* — length never inflates a rating here. **The two ways to actually ruin this brisket are both decisions made before the fire is lit:** salting it twice (the warning above) and buying a trimmed, fatless brisket ([§6.7](67-texas-style-barbecued-brisket.md) is blunt about that one). Shopping mistakes, not technique failures.

> ⏱️ **The honest limitation, in his own words — and it's why there's a second brisket recipe.** Cody's stated objection to this method is not the flavor and not the difficulty. It's that **with a straight smoke, he has no control over when it gets done.** A brisket comes off at a temperature, not at a time ([§T42 What Controls Cooking Time](t42-what-controls-cooking-time.md) — thickness, not weight, drives it), the stall can add hours nobody predicted, and if dinner is at seven the brisket does not care. A [faux Cambro](t43-faux-cambro--holding-meat-hot-for-hours.md) absorbs *some* of that, but only in one direction: it can hold a brisket that finished early, and it can do nothing at all about one that finishes late. **[§6.10 Sous Vide Brisket (Richie's Method)](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) is his answer to exactly this problem** — two days in a bath at a fixed temperature, then a chill, then a scheduled four-hour smoke, so the finish lands when he wants it to. **This entry buys the better bark; that one buys the schedule.** Both are his and neither replaces the other.

#### A. Ingredients

- **1 brisket** — Cody didn't name a size or a grade for this method *(see Open Questions)*. **The buying rule this cookbook already carries is [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md)'s:** a **whole packer runs 8 to 16 lb**, and you should **buy the highest grade you can afford — USDA Choice, Prime, or Wagyu — and handpick the slab with the most marbling.** An unlabeled brisket is probably Select; leave it. **Untrimmed, with the fat cap on.**
- **Kosher salt** — **a heavy amount**, for the overnight dry brine, and **no measured quantity, because Cody doesn't use one.** He salts by hand out of the salt bowl and **he runs a heavier dry brine than the books do** — his standing practice, written up at [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md). *(A figure to start from if you want one: §T37 puts ~½ tsp per pound as a* **floor** *, and Cody deliberately goes past it.)*
- **Coarse ground black pepper** — the whole seasoning, and he means coarse: *"it has never let me down."* **This is the unsalted half of Path A above.**
- **Smoking wood — pecan.** **A handful — a palmful, a couple of chunks, and no more** ([§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md)). Pecan is his favorite ([§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md) records the same preference).
- **Heavy-duty aluminum foil** — **only if you're wrapping.** See Step 5; half the time he doesn't.

*Not groceries, but the cook doesn't happen without them: a **smoker or a kamado set up for indirect heat**, a **leave-in probe thermometer** (this recipe is run entirely on internal temperature), and a **cooler** for the rest.*

#### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. The night before — dry brine. Plain salt, heavy, and into the fridge overnight.**
Coat the brisket in **kosher salt** — a real handful, every surface, into the seams — and put it in the refrigerator **overnight**. That's the night's work. **This is a dry brine and it is the foundation of the whole recipe**: the salt pulls moisture to the surface, dissolves in it, and carries back into the meat seasoned, while the surface dries out so it can take bark instead of steaming. **Going heavy is deliberate and it's right on a cut this size** — [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md)'s own numbers say salt travels only about ⅔ of an inch in a full day, so most of a big packer's interior never sees any of it. The real ceiling is toughening the proteins, not saltiness. **⚠️ And this is Path A above: if you salt here, whatever you season with tomorrow must be UNSALTED.** *(A **wire rack over a sheet pan, uncovered**, is how Cody runs the same step for [§6.9 Cody's Pulled Pork](69-codys-pulled-pork.md) and it's the standard way to do it — noted as this cookbook's suggestion, since for the brisket he said only "salt it and put it in the fridge overnight.")*

**2. Next day — coarse ground black pepper. That's the seasoning.**
**Coarse ground black pepper over everything, and nothing else.** Cody's line on it is flat and unqualified: ***"it has never let me down."*** Not a rub, not a blend, not a shortcut — a heavy hand of coarse black pepper on a heavily salted brisket is Texas's own answer to this cut, and it is what he keeps coming back to. **Coarse matters:** fine-ground pepper dissolves into the surface and scorches over twelve hours, while a coarse crack stays granular, builds physical texture into the bark, and holds its aroma. **This is the unsalted seasoning the warning above demands** — pepper carries no salt, so it stacks on top of last night's brine without doubling anything.

> 🌶️ **If you'd rather use a rub — what's already in this cookbook, and what he's actually tried.** **The Meathead rubs here are all salt-free by design** ([§T53](t53-the-science-of-a-good-rub--three-ss-no-salt-in-rubs-and-storage.md)), which makes them drop-in replacements for the pepper in Path A: [§4.107 Mrs. O'Leary's Cow Crust](4107-mrs-olearys-cow-crust.md) and [§4.165 Red Meat Rub](4165-red-meat-rub.md) are both built for beef, and [§4.116 Butcher Block Seasoning](4116-butcher-block-seasoning.md) is the one this cookbook now points at wherever a beef rub is called for. **Meathead's Big Bad Beef Rub is deliberately not among them: Cody doesn't like it, and asked for it to be removed from this cookbook** *(2026-09-08 — see [`CHANGELOG.md`](../../CHANGELOG.md))*. **On Raichlen: the rubs in *The Barbecue! Bible* and *How to Grill* are typically great, in his experience — but he has not used their beef brisket one.** So take that as a general endorsement of those books' rubs, not a recommendation of the brisket seasoning specifically. *(For the record, the one he's read is [§6.7 Texas-Style Barbecued Brisket](67-texas-style-barbecued-brisket.md)'s — he signed off on it on the page, *"the seasoning and letting it dry brine is OK, it's all real good,"* but that's a read, not a cook. **And it has salt in it**, so it's a Path B rub — night before, no separate brine.)*

**3. Fire the pit to 225°F and then leave it alone for an hour. Don't rush this.**
Bring the cooker to a steady **225°F**, set up for **indirect heat** ([§T109](t109-indirect-heat--putting-something-between-the-fire-and-the-food.md) — on a Big Green Egg that's the convEGGtor in), and then **let it sit there for a full hour before anything goes on it.** Cody is specific about the hour and it earns its place twice over. **First, the cooker itself has to settle**: ceramic and steel take a long time to come to equilibrium, and a pit that reads 225°F at the dome ten minutes after lighting is still climbing. Set the vents, walk away, come back, and see whether it's still at 225°F — that's the number you can trust. **Second, the fire has to get clean**, which is Step 4.

**4. A handful of pecan — then WAIT FOR THE BLUE SMOKE. The bitter smoke burns off first.**
**A handful of wood. A palmful. A couple of chunks and no more** — that's Cody's standing rule for every pit he lights, written up at [§T35's *Cody's rule — don't overload the pit with wood*](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md), and he's emphatic that more genuinely tastes too smoky rather than richer. **Pecan is his wood**; hickory is the standard alternative across his cooking. **Then wait.** Fresh wood put on a fire first smolders and throws thick, billowing white or gray smoke, and **that early smoke is the bitter, acrid stuff** — creosote and unburned particulates. **It burns off.** Give it a few minutes and the smoke thins out to a faint, almost invisible **blue** haze, which is the clean combustion you actually want, and the only smoke that makes good barbecue. **The meat does not go on until you see it.** Putting a brisket into white smoke is how a twelve-hour cook ends up tasting like an ashtray, and there is no fixing it afterward — the flavor is in the bark to stay. The full science is at [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md); the practical version is **thin blue smoke, then the meat.**

**5. On it goes. Probe to 165°F, let it stall — then wrap in foil, OR don't wrap at all. Both are Cody's, and they are a real choice.**
The brisket goes on the indirect side with a **leave-in probe thermometer** in the thickest part, and from here the recipe is run entirely on internal temperature. Somewhere around **150–165°F** it hits **the stall**: the number stops moving, sometimes for hours, because evaporative cooling off the wet surface is matching the heat going in ([§T33](t33-how-meat-actually-cooks--conduction-carryover-and-why-resting-is-a-myth.md)). **That is normal, it is not a broken thermometer, and it is not a reason to raise the pit temperature.** At that point Cody does one of two things, and this cookbook is not going to pretend one of them is a footnote:

> | | **Wrap it — the Texas crutch** | **Don't wrap it — the Meathead way** |
> |---|---|---|
> | **What you do** | At about **165°F**, pull it and **wrap tightly in heavy foil**, then back on until it's done | **Nothing.** It rides bare on the grate the whole way |
> | **What it buys** | **Speed and control.** Foil stops the evaporation that causes the stall, so the temperature climbs again and the finish becomes roughly predictable | **A better bark.** In Cody's words, *"Meathead doesn't wrap his meat, because it will give you an even better bark"* |
> | **What it costs** | **The bark softens.** Steam trapped against the crust undoes some of what twelve hours built | **Time you can't predict.** An unwrapped stall runs long, and it decides when dinner is |
> | **Use it when** | The clock matters | The bark matters |
>
> **Cody does both, depending on the day, and neither is the "real" version.** If you wrap, wrap it *tight* so it doesn't leak, and put the probe in from up high so juice doesn't run out the hole. If you don't wrap, plan on the longer end of everything and accept that you're cooking on the brisket's schedule — which is precisely the limitation that sent him to [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md).

**6. Take it to 203°F, then rest it.**
**203°F is Cody's number and it is not 195°F.** He applies it across everything he smokes — recorded in his own words at [§6.9 Cody's Pulled Pork](69-codys-pulled-pork.md): *"a lot of literature says 195 or 200. I cook it to 203. And I do that with all of my briskets and my meat… 203 guarantees that all of the collagen melts into liquid, into savory liquid."* That's correct and it's what this cookbook's own table says too ([§T44](t44-food-safety--the-real-logic-and-the-target-temperature-table.md) lists brisket, ribs and pork shoulder at 203°F — deliberately past done, for the connective tissue rather than for doneness). **Probe in more than one spot**; a packer's flat and point do not finish together, and the real cue is that the probe slides in with almost no resistance. **Then rest it in a cooler** — this cookbook's [faux Cambro](t43-faux-cambro--holding-meat-hot-for-hours.md), an empty cooler with **no ice in it**, holding the heat in. *(Cody didn't state a rest time for the brisket — see Open Questions. [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md) holds a whole packer **at least 2 hours** and [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md) rests his pork butts 1 to 3 hours, so the shape of it is well established here even though the number isn't his.)* **⚠️ No ice. That cooler is the opposite of [§3 Darcy's Steak](3-darcys-steak.md)'s, which is packed with it.**

**7. Slice it across the grain, at the last minute.**
Brisket dries out fast once it's open, so **cut it as you serve it, not before.** The flat and the point have grains running in different directions, which is why [§T70 Slicing Brisket](t70-slicing-brisket--the-easy-way-vs-the-sorkin-way.md) exists — it gives both the easy way (separate the two muscles and slice each across its own grain) and the Sorkin way (trim the dry inch off the thin end, cut out the fat wedge between the muscles, slice the flat pencil-thick, then turn 45° for the point). **If the first slice falls apart, cut thicker slices.**

#### C. Grocery Shopping List

**🏪 Specific store — butcher**

- 🏪 Brisket — **untrimmed, fat cap on**; whole packers run **8 to 16 lb** and this cookbook's buying rule is [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md)'s: **USDA Choice, Prime, or Wagyu, handpicked for marbling.** Unlabeled almost certainly means Select — leave it *(Cody didn't specify a size or grade for this method; see Open Questions)*

**🛒 General grocery**

- 🛒 Kosher salt — a full box; it goes on heavy *(the salt bowl, per [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md))*
- 🛒 **Coarse ground black pepper — buy plenty**, and buy it coarse *(a whole brisket wants more than a spice-jar's worth; whole peppercorns and a coarse grinder setting are better still)*
- 🛒 Smoking wood — **pecan chunks** *(hickory is the standard alternative. Buy chunks, not chips, and buy fewer than you think — a cook takes **a palmful**, per [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md))*
- 🛒 Heavy-duty aluminum foil — **only if you're wrapping** *(Step 5)*

#### Nutrition *(estimated — and built on an assumed brisket size, because none was given)*

**Cody didn't name a weight for this one**, so the figures below are computed on a **12 lb untrimmed whole packer** — the same size [§7.112 Texas Beef Brisket](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md) uses, chosen deliberately so the two brisket entries in this cookbook are comparable rather than each running on its own private assumption. **Scale linearly for a different brisket**; a 16-pounder is a third more of everything. *(Labeled as an assumption per [CLAUDE.md §3b](../../CLAUDE.md), and flagged in Open Questions.)*

| | Calories | Fat | Protein | Carbs | Fiber |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Whole dish** *(a 12 lb packer, as eaten)* | ~9,000 | 620 g | 720 g | 2 g | 1 g |
| **Per serving** *(serves 12)* | ~750 | 52 g | 60 g | 0.2 g | 0.1 g |

**What a serving is:** about **6 oz of sliced brisket**, mixing lean flat and fatty point — a dinner portion on a plate, or the meat in one good sandwich.

**How these were figured.** From the ingredient list, not lab figures. **Only what's eaten is counted.** A 12 lb untrimmed packer loses a great deal of its raw weight before it reaches a plate: fat renders out into the pit over twelve hours, the cook trims more off, and the meat shrinks — roughly **4½ lb of sliced brisket** actually gets served, which is where the 12 six-ounce portions come from. **The salt and pepper are counted and they are essentially the entire carb and fiber column** — a few grams of black pepper across a whole brisket, and that's it. There is no sugar in this recipe, no sauce, and nothing else edible in the method; the wood and the foil contribute nothing. **The numbers are deliberately in line with [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md)'s**, since it's the same cut at the same size cooked to the same internal temperature — the difference between the two recipes is seasoning and technique, not calories.

#### D. Open Questions

- **What size brisket, and what grade?** Cody described the method without naming the meat — no weight, no packer-vs-flat, no grade. The entry runs on [§T69](t69-brisket-basics--anatomy-of-a-whole-packer-brisket.md)'s general buying rule and prices the Nutrition block on an assumed 12 lb packer, both labeled as such. **His own answer would replace both.**
- **How long does it actually take, on his pit?** He gave the temperature (225°F) and the milestones (165°F, then 203°F), but no clock. **The ~12–14 hr in the badge is cookbook judgment, not his** — it's taken from [§7.112 Texas Beef Brisket](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md), Meathead's own whole-packer method at the identical 225°F, whose printed TAKES line reads 12 to 14 hours; Cody says outright that his method *is* basically Meathead's. **Per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md), that is a labeled fill from a named source already in this cookbook, and his figure supersedes it the day he gives one.** Note also that an **unwrapped** brisket (Step 5) runs longer than a wrapped one, and that the whole point of his complaint about this method is that the number isn't predictable anyway.
- **How long is the rest?** Not stated for the brisket. Step 6 gives the shape of it from [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md) (at least 2 hours in a faux Cambro) and [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md) (his own 1-to-3-hour cooler rest for pork butts), both labeled — but the number for *his* brisket is open.
- **Does he trim the fat cap?** He didn't say. Worth asking, because his answer for pork is emphatic and might carry over: **he does not trim the pork butt's cap at all** ([§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md)). [§T40](t40-the-fat-cap--trim-or-not.md) is the book's general guidance and [§7.112](7112-texas-beef-brisket.md) trims to about ¼ inch; neither is recorded as Cody's practice on brisket.
- **Fat side up or down?** Also unstated here. His pork rule is **fat side up, and for the practical reason** — fat side down welds to the grate ([§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md), [§T40](t40-the-fat-cap--trim-or-not.md)) — but he didn't say it about brisket, so it isn't written into Step 5 as his.
- **A water pan, or coffee cups of water?** [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md) records that he tucks coffee cups of water into the Egg for pulled pork and that it makes a real difference. Whether he does the same for brisket is unrecorded, and it isn't assumed here.
- **The Barbecue! Bible / How to Grill beef brisket rub — untested.** He rates those books' rubs highly in general but says he hasn't used their beef brisket one, so it's recorded as an untried option rather than a recommendation.
